newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Foreign firms return gingerly to South Africa.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms return gingerly to South Africa.

text.p: The return to South Africa of U.S. tyre giant Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co is the latest overseas investment in a country which was shunned under the white-run apartheid system.
Goodyear, in a tie-up with Angovaal Industries Ltd, said on Monday it was buying 60 percent of local tyre marker Contred for $121 million including assumed debt.
The move brings back the Goodyear brand after the firm disinvested from South Africa in 1989.
In the past two months other U.S. firms such as industrial firm Owens Corning and drugs group American Home Products have also bought back past investments.
The country's first all-race elections in 1994 opened the country to investment and economists said on Tuesday companies were using South Africa as a gateway to the rest of Africa.
South Africa has a rare advantage in sub-Saharan Africa of a developed banking infrastructure and telecommunciations network.

"If a firm has an interest in operating in sub-Saharan Africa then the infrastructure and telecommunications in South Africa are probably far superior to anywhere else in the region," said David Perlstein, head partner of corporate finance at Ernst & Young.
Certainly this is the thinking behind Goodyear's deal.
"Contred provides Goodyear with a powerful platform from which to seek opportunities in the African continent," said Goodyear chairman Samir Gibara.
In 1994 inward foreign investment to South Africa totalled 821 million rand ($177 million). In 1995 this figure jumped to 3.7 billion rand and 1996 is set to hit similar heights.
"This year is likely to be in that region (3.7 billion rand) again," according to Perlstein, whose company produces an authoritative survey of investment trends.
But most foreign deals so far, including Goodyear, have only won back former brands or bought-in to existing firms.
The African National Congress-led government of Nelson Mandela wants to attract "greenfield" investment to help cut the burgeoning ranks of South Africa's unemployed.
To date, such projects have been thin on the ground.

Economists said there had to be more progress on economic reform before the investment flood gates opened. "What we really want is new foreign direct investment, not just buy-ins and franchise deals," said one economist who declined to be named.

Many firms are put off by South Africa's high wages relative to other developing markets, industrial unrest and twin fears of political instability and a rampant crime wave that has earned the industrial capital Johannesburg an unenviable reputation as one of the most dangerous cities on earth.
The government needs to curb crime and create an economic climate that will soothe investor fears, economists said.

The international business community welcomed a market-friendly macro-economic plan announced earlier this year, containing tax breaks for firms seeking to set up new plants in labour-intensive industries.

But economists said the government needed to turn the plan's good intentions into action. "The government is moving in the right direction, but whether we see a flood of foreign investment depends on how fast it moves," one economist said.
The biggest outside investment in South Africa so far is Malaysian oil company Petronas' 1.9 billion rand investment in Engen Ltd, made earlier this year.

That could be topped soon if the government succeeds in selling up to 30 percent of state-run telecommunications giant Telkom to a foreign equity partner, in a deal estimated to be be worth around six billion rand.
Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom, Telekom Malaysia and SBC Communications have been shortlisted for the stake and government hopes to conclude the sale by the end of next March.
Economists said a successful Telkom deal -- the first major step in South Africa's cautious privatisation programme -- could pave the way for a lot more foreign investment in 1997.
